hlido_opinion.headline: Actively maintained Go SDK for stateful, voice-capable agents — clean repo hygiene, but no drop-in agent-consumable surface documented.
hlido_opinion.body: flowcraft presents itself as a production-grade Go SDK for building agents with long-term memory, knowledge retrieval and a voice pipeline, runnable as a library, a daemon or a real-time stream. On the repo signals we can measure it holds up well: MIT-licensed, 486 stars, a tagged release, CI workflows present, and a push the same day we captured it — this is a live project, not an abandoned experiment. Go is a sensible choice for a long-running agent daemon where concurrency and a single static binary matter. The one gap the engine flagged is real: nothing in the repository documents an agent-consumable surface (no MCP config, no CLI-install recipe surfaced), so another agent can't yet drive flowcraft without a developer wiring the SDK in first. That keeps it a library you build with, not a component an agent picks up autonomously. For a Go team that wants memory and voice primitives under one roof, it is a credible starting point; treat the 'voice' framing as one capability among several rather than the headline.

tier_rationale: STEADY (82) because the repository is healthy on every hygiene axis we measure — permissive licence, active maintenance, releases, CI, real star traction — which is what the repo-surface track rewards. Held below VITAL by the repo-surface ceiling (no hands-on run) and by the missing agent-consumable documentation, the single failed checklist item.
what_it_does_well: MIT-licensed with a tagged release — clear terms and a versioned artefact to pin
Actively maintained: last push the same day as capture, CI workflows in place
Real community traction (486 stars) for a niche infrastructure library
Go gives a single static binary and solid concurrency for a long-running agent daemon
what_it_fails_at: No agent-consumable surface documented (no MCP config or CLI-install recipe found) — a developer must wire the SDK in by hand
Not hands-on tested — memory, retrieval and voice quality are unverified beyond the README
Voice is marketed prominently but is one capability among several, not a proven differentiator
best_for: Go teams that want memory + retrieval + voice primitives in one library
Developers comfortable integrating an SDK rather than consuming a ready endpoint
Projects that need a long-running agent daemon as a static binary
not_recommended_for: Agents that need to self-integrate without a developer wiring the SDK
Buyers wanting a hands-on-verified voice product rather than a framework
